KEY MESSAGE 1: Rain from possible thunderstorms late this 
afternoon and evening could be locally very heavy over the 
Laurel Highlands and South- Central Mountains. There is still 
potential for some heavy rain to fall over the Lower Susquehanna
Valley and Central Ridge-and-Valley region.

11 AM Update...
Basically, nothing has changed in the forecast for the next 24
hours. Clouds remain in place overhead as the morning slug of 
rain moves off to the east. While we did not get the heaviest
rainfall possible as we lacked deep convection this morning. We
still picked up 0.25" or so in the watch area, priming the
ground, but probably not making any rises in the creeks and
streams yet. We will (still) need to get rid of the clouds to 
get enough heating for the convection currently in far wrn OH to
survive into Central PA, and even to continue to move through 
the region. Clearing is already up to the PA/OH border at 11 AM.
Thunderstorms are most-possible (likely) in the western 
counties where clearing is most possible. The storms are 
generally expected to move along steadily, but some 
training/multiple storms are possible, still. So, we'll continue
the watch. SPC outlook has not changed at all, either, with the
possibility of severe winds (and even a tiny chc of a tornado)
there in the SW part of the CWA, too.

Previous...
An area of moderate to briefly heavy rain from weakening Ohio 
Valley TSRA was approaching the Laurel Highlands at 0830Z. MRMS
3 hour rainfall estimates indicate that this area of rain will
amount to 0.3-0.5 of an inch across the Laurel Highlands, north
to Clearfield County and similar or slightly lower amounts by
the time it reaches Fulton and Franklin counties in Scent PA. 

North of the Interstate 80 Corridor across Central PA, the 
Middle Susq Valley and its West Branch Valley, rainfall this
morning will likely be between 0.10 and 0.25. 

After a several hour or more break in the significant rainfall
(~13Z-18Z when only around 0.10-0.15 of an inch of rain is
expected) peak instability and a llvl Theta-E convergence max
near a NE advancing warm front across far SW PA and the Laurel 
Highlands will be the primary ingredients for two or more rounds
of TSRA, which could lead to a quick 1-2 inches of rainfall.

Previous, still valid disc points follow below -  

PWATs get above 2" as the brunt of the morning convection dives
into MD. The first forecast issue is just how far north the 
heaviest precip will track. Some recent guidance does indicate a
swath of heavy rain being possible north of the first 
(southern) tier of counties in the morning. FFG over much of 
Somerset and Cambria Counties is close to 1"/hr. While a little 
more drying is expected before the rain arrives there, the FFG 
will likely still be close to being that low when it starts 
raining. The initial slug of thunderstorms will cross the 
southern tier by 10 or 11 AM. While this first slug may not be 
enough straw to break the camel's back, the piece that may do it
and make flash flooding may arrive in the afternoon. WPC ERO 
SLGT risk is well into the CWA, even up almost to Route 6 across
the nrn tier. 

As alluded to...there will _probably_ be a second surge of 
instability and lift during the late afternoon and evening. The 
certainty of this second round of storms is dependent on the 
erosion of a stable layer which will likely form after the first
batch of rain moves through in the morning. If we do break out 
and get the necessary sun/heating, we should see more tall and 
wet storms. However, the NAM and GFS paint a layer of sfc/llvl 
stability/CIN until very late in the day at KUNV as an example 
and over much of the CWA. The FFG is also a bit higher, and 
ground able to handle a little more rain, on the whole, over the
eastern counties. Thus, in collaboration with our neighboring 
offices, we have posted a Flash Flood Watch for Sunday. However,
we have started a little smaller than what we view as the 
potentially-eventually threatened area. It was a tough decision,
with confidence in both the threat area and timing/redevelopment
low. Later shifts will be able to evaluate newer guidance as the
time window closes. 

The threat for heavy rain ends by midnight. So, we have decided
to cover both periods of potentially heavy rain with one watch.
While it does stretch across a span of time in mid- day and 
early afternoon when no heavy rain should occur, the time span 
is pretty short in length.

Additionally, the potential for strong to severe storms exists
as long as we have unstable conditions. The hodographs in the
morning are actually well-curved in the south/southwest, but
have just a meager LLJet. Shear is stronger in the late
aftn/evening. Wind damage is the most probable severe threat,
but a spinning storm or two is possible.
